title: Where Olist breaks its delivery promise, and what to fix first
speaker: AJ
say: Every Olist customer sees a promised delivery date at checkout. We asked three questions: where does Olist break that promise, what does a broken promise cost, and what should Olist fix first. We built the whole answer in Databricks, from the raw files to three dashboards, and every number you will see is calculated in SQL.

title: One promise, three datasets
speaker: AJ
say: We combined three datasets from two publishers: about one hundred thousand Olist marketplace orders from 2016 to 2018, Olist's marketing funnel of sellers who asked to join, and IBGE, Brazil's statistics office, for the population of each state. We judge a promise only once its day has passed inside the data, which leaves 95,901 orders. 8.6 percent of them broke their promise.

title: From 13 files to three dashboards
speaker: Ruby
say: This is the pipeline, left to right. Bronze holds the 13 files exactly as downloaded, every CSV column as text, and we checked their hashes against Kaggle and IBGE. We apply 31 cleaning rules and set aside the rows we cannot trust. Gold is a star schema: one fact row per order, one per item, and four dimensions. A metric view holds the rates a filter must recalculate; the route and state rates are stored in Gold and checked against it on every build. The dashboards do no calculation at all.

title: Four traps the data set for us
speaker: Ruby
say: Four problems would have changed our answer. First, the promised date has no time of day, so comparing timestamps calls 1,292 on-time deliveries late; we compare days. Second, joins on the wrong grain: items joined to payments add 4.6 percent to item value, and customers joined to locations turn 99 thousand rows into 15 million. Third, 547 orders have more than one review; we keep the latest, so no order is counted twice. Fourth, deliveries stop being recorded after August 2018, so a promise made for September would look broken. We stop the window at August 31.

title: Broken promises draw a third of the bad reviews
speaker: Merna
say: Dashboard 1 is for the Head of Customer Experience. 8.6 percent of the orders we judge broke their promise, but they make up 36.7 percent of the orders in our window with a one or two star review, canceled ones included. The chart on the left shows the score holding while parcels arrive early and falling right after the promised day. The chart on the right compares orders delivered in the same week: the late ones score lower in every band, so customers react to the broken promise, not only to speed. And 70 percent of the late parcels with a review were reviewed before they arrived, at 1.65 stars. These are correlations, but they point at a cheap test: tell the customer about the delay before the review survey goes out.

title: One route breaks more promises than the next nine together
speaker: AJ
say: Dashboard 2 is for the Head of Logistics, and it ends in a ranked list. We rank routes, seller state to customer state, by excess broken promises: how many more than the national rate predicts. Sao Paulo to Rio de Janeiro comes first, 17.1 percent broken, 678 above expected. That is more than the next nine routes together, 637. Five of the top ten go into the Northeast. Each route also gets a fix type from a rule in SQL, which the next slide explains.

title: Two kinds of fix, and a promise 3 days later is not one
speaker: AJ
say: Three months were different: November 2017, February and March 2018. They hold 22 percent of orders but 43 percent of broken promises, so some routes need a busy-season plan. But the Northeast breaks promises in ordinary months too, so some routes need a lasting fix. Sao Paulo to Rio needs both. The obvious idea, promising three days later, only takes the rate from 8.6 to 6.6 percent. And 72 percent of the late parcels from one seller reached the carrier by the seller's deadline, so most of the delay happens after the handover.

title: Rio: high demand, few sellers per resident
speaker: Merna
say: Dashboard 3 is for the Head of Seller Acquisition. Using IBGE's population, Rio buys 56 orders per hundred thousand residents, the third highest after Sao Paulo's 72 and the Federal District's 57, but it has 8.5 active sellers per million against 35, and 91.5 percent of its single-seller orders come from another state. When a Rio customer buys from a Rio seller, 7.7 percent of promises break and the median delivery takes 5 days, against 17.1 percent and 13 days from Sao Paulo. Most of that gap comes from the busy months; in ordinary months it is 8.7 against 10.0 percent, but local sellers are still much faster. Yet the funnel recruits where sellers already are: Rio got only 6.8 percent of the recruits who sold. Local sellers may sell different products, so a pilot has to prove the speed.

title: Can we trust it? Every check is on the dashboard
speaker: Ruby
say: Dashboard 2 has a second page, Can we trust it. Twenty-four pipeline checks run on every build: every order, item, payment and review row lands in Silver or in quarantine, every key holds, no join inflates money, the stored rates agree with the metric view, and the days are the days written in the files. All pass. Only 3 of 415 thousand order, item, payment and review rows were set aside. A view recomputes all 56 results printed in our design document from Gold, and all match. The same page shows the fairness check: Northeast customers get worse service, 15.6 against 7.8 percent, and we show that gap with its margin instead of hiding it.

title: What Olist should do next
speaker: AJ
say: Three actions, one per reader. Customer Experience: test a delay notice with a new date, sent before the review survey to customers whose parcel will miss. Logistics: review the carrier and transit days on Sao Paulo to Rio first, and book extra capacity before the busy months. Seller Acquisition: run a measured recruiting pilot in Rio, and check whether local sellers really deliver faster for the same products.

title: What the data cannot tell us
speaker: Merna
say: Four limits. The links between promises and reviews are correlations. The data has no carrier name or tracking, so why Sao Paulo to Rio breaks is a question for Olist's carriers. We found the busy months in the same data, so that rule must be checked on new months. And deliveries stop being recorded after August 2018, so we deliver a pipeline a monthly refresh would rerun, not a list for today. Thank you; we are happy to take questions.
